title: 3 best incident management tools for B2B support teams | Pylon
summary: Compare the best incident management tools for B2B support teams, and learn how to connect platforms like Rootly and PagerDuty to your support queue.
body_markdown:
When an outage brings customer requests in through Slack, Teams, email, and chat, your support team needs to know which reports belong together and what engineering has found. Incident management tools can help coordinate the resolution, as long as they offer clear connections between that response and each customer conversation.


In this guide, we’ll explain how to pick an incident management tool that fits your support workflow and fosters[strong B2B relationships](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-build-relationship-with-customers) .


## What incident management tools do for support teams


When something goes wrong, incident management software helps your[B2B support team](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/b2b-customer-service-best-practices-strategies) alert the right people, coordinate their response, communicate progress, and review what happened afterward. Your dev team can coordinate service recovery, while support manages customer reports and keeps affected accounts informed.


This makes[incident management](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/incident-management) different from ordinary ticket handling. A standard[ticketing system](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/what-is-ticketing-system) records each customer’s request individually, but one incident could explain similar requests from dozens of accounts. Linking those records helps you see the shared problem, without losing the details each customer needs.


For example, if three customers report failed imports in separate channels and on the same day, your team can check for a shared incident. Then they can add account evidence and follow up after recovery.[Pylon’s support platform](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/pylon-becomes-the-agentic-support-platform) helps you connect all this work through integrations with top incident management tools like Rootly and PagerDuty.


## What to look for in an incident management tool


Chat integrations in Pylon


The best incident management software will make the handoff to engineering clear and give support enough information to stay accountable to customers. Look for these key features before settling on a tool:


- **Selective escalation.** You should be able to notify a team member about a customer issue that meets certain conditions, without having to send every urgent-looking communication to the on-call team.
- **Real-time data sharing.** When you can collect reports across accounts, you keep separate conversations attached to the same investigation.
- **Detailed status visibility.** Confirm where support can find important information like the incident’s owner, current status, and next update.
- **Customer impact reporting.** It should be easy to find affected accounts and the support work an incident created, alongside engineering’s response metrics.
- **Native Slack workflows.** If your teams[coordinate in Slack](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/slack-customer-support-system) , check to see how people can share updates and bring customer context into the response.
- **Robust support integrations.** Find out what support integrations are offered and what they can actually do. For example, incident.io’s Pylon integration supports ticket views filtered by incident and incident-related reporting, along with separate automated workflows for linked tickets.

### 1. incident.io


[incident.io](http://incident.io/) brings on-call work and incident response into one platform. You get scheduling management tools to keep your team working efficiently without burnout, plus incident workflows that can be both customized and automated.


This[platform’s Pylon integration](https://www.usepylon.com/integrations/incident-io) lets your team connect customer issues to incidents, then review the resulting support volume. You can also build trigger-based workflows for incident-linked issues, so escalations, updates, and routing all happen automatically.


**Best for:** Teams that want to clearly see which customer conversations belong to an incident.


### 2. Rootly


[Rootly](https://rootly.com/) takes an AI-native approach to incident management, offering plenty of tools that can be integrated into streamlined workflows. This tool includes built-in scheduling, complex and customizable escalation policies, workflow automation, and AI responders.


[Rootly’s Pylon integration](https://www.usepylon.com/integrations/rootly) supports linking existing incidents and creating new ones through custom triggers. You can then filter support views by incident and report on the related tickets.


[Rootly even uses Pylon](https://www.usepylon.com/case-study/rootly) for its own support workflows. Plus, its complexity makes it a good Opsgenie alternative for teams moving away from that platform (which is scheduled to shut down in April 2027).


**Best for:** Teams that want customer issue conditions to start incident responses automatically.


### 3. PagerDuty


[PagerDuty](https://www.pagerduty.com/platform/incident-management/) organizes alerting, on-call escalation, and incident response. It’s a more streamlined tool that focuses on scheduling and automated escalations. This platform supports multiple channels and offers a mobile app for added convenience.


With[PagerDuty’s Pylon integration](https://www.usepylon.com/integrations/pagerduty) , you can use custom triggers to create an incident for a selected service when a support issue meets your criteria. This alerts the right people quickly and gives them the context they need to start working on a resolution immediately.


**Best for:** Teams that need a direct route from a qualifying customer issue to the on-call team.


## How to connect incident management to your support workflow


Issue view in Pylon


Strong incident management should be grounded in a clear, repeatable process. Here’s how to get started:


1. **Define which customer issues need escalation:** A failed import that blocks production could need immediate escalation, while a question about how imports work belongs in the normal queue. Write out all the conditions in your[incident response playbook](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/incident-response-playbook) , including the affected service and the person responsible for customer communication.
2. **Configure and test the trigger:** Install the relevant integration, then[build your rule](https://support.usepylon.com/articles/5297911855-incident) around the conditions you identified. Review incident triggers while disabled, then run a controlled test before enabling them.
3. **Link related customer tickets:** Once you know several reports share a cause, connect them to the existing incident. Keep account-specific details on each ticket, and use your[issue management system](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/issues-management-system) to track any work that remains after service recovers.
4. **Establish how support gets progress updates:** Give your support lead access to the incident channel or record, and agree on when engineering will share updates. Also, decide who translates those updates into customer-facing language, so everyone knows what’s happening and what the next steps are.
5. **Follow up with affected customers:** Use the incident’s linked-ticket view as your follow-up list.[Customer support automation](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/customer-support-automation) can route this work, but assign someone to confirm that each account got the right response and any remaining issue has an owner.
6. **Review the customer impact:** Compare incident-related ticket volume, affected accounts, and follow-up completion with your response timeline. Use those findings to improve escalation rules and spot recurring problems that need longer-term fixes.

## FAQ


### What are the seven stages of incident management?


The seven-stage incident management workflow includes detection, recording, prioritization, investigation, response, recovery, and review. Teams group these activities differently, but whatever your process looks like, be sure to include customer communication throughout.


### What are five types of incidents?


Five common types of support incidents are service outages, degraded performance, failed integrations, data integrity problems, and security incidents. These categories can overlap, so classify each incident by its impact and route it to the team most qualified to respond.


### How can Slack be used in incident management?


During a support incident, Slack can give responders a shared channel for coordination and updates. Connected tools help your team create and escalate incidents in one streamlined workflow, so keep incident records and customer tickets linked.
